paper_title: Cola2: Co-Adaptive Hierarchical Language Modeling with Continuous Semantic Compression and Balanced Discrete Generation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Hierarchical language generation separates continuous semantic modeling from discrete text realization, but its effectiveness depends on what the latent space compresses and how the discrete generator uses it. We propose Cola2, a framework that jointly studies continuous semantic compression, the balance between reconstruction and generation, and continuous-discrete co-adaptation. Cola2 dynamically segments text into semantic spans, controls the compression rate through auxiliary-loss-free negative feedback, and combines reconstruction and generation supervision to learn compact, predictive latent representations. A block-causal masked diffusion decoder is trained with clean, noisy, and dropped latent conditions, while classifier-free guidance adjusts the balance between semantic reconstruction and autonomous generation. Token-prediction gradients update the encoder through the latents, whereas Flow Matching prior learning is decoupled from representation learning by stop-gradient. During inference, generated text is re-encoded under a fixed span layout to keep the latent history consistent with the actual text context. Experiments on five downstream tasks with about 210 billion training tokens validate the core designs and show competitive, unsaturated scaling. With 346.03 billion source tokens, an unconverged checkpoint reaches a 60.10 average across eight tasks and surpasses Llama-3-8B on HellaSwag and StoryCloze despite its reported pretraining budget being over 43 times larger. These results demonstrate the potential of continuous-latent hierarchical language generation.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Large language models (LLMs) have made remarkable progress under the autoregressive (AR) paradigm [6, 43], but the fixed left-to-right generation order imposes an inherent serial dependency on inference. Diffusion language models (DLMs) [1, 2, 34, 41] offer new way to break this constraint. Cola DLM [13] further decomposes text generation into semantic organization in continuous latent space and text realization in discrete space; through latent prior modeling and conditional decoding, it provides viable path toward hierarchical language generation beyond direct token modeling. However, structural division between continuous and discrete spaces does not automatically yield an effective division of labor. The key questions are what information the latent space should compress and how the discrete generator should use it. Shortening the latent sequence is not equivalent to obtaining compact semantic representation, and reconstruction-only objective does not guarantee that the latents can predict missing or future text [19, 24, 29]. Meanwhile, the decoder must not only faithfully realize the latent semantics, but also generate the remaining content from the text context when the latent condition is incomplete or imprecise [44]. Semantic compression and discrete generation therefore cannot be designed independently: the information the latents should retain must be determined jointly with the information the decoder can complete. This interdependence further raises the question of how continuous and discrete representations should be learned jointly. Fixing the encoder in advance determines the information carried by the latents before the discrete generator is fully learned, limiting the continual adaptation of the representation to decoding needs. At the same time, letting the latent-prior fitting objective directly shape the encoder may push the latents toward directions that are easier to fit but not necessarily more beneficial for discrete generation. Hierarchical language modeling thus requires not only learning continuous representations and discrete generator, but also specifying which objectives should jointly shape the representation and which learning processes should remain decoupled. To address these issues, we propose Cola2, which jointly studies continuous semantic compression, the discrete reconstructiongeneration balance, and their co-adaptation within unified hierarchical language modeling framework. Its core idea is that, under limited latent capacity, the actual demands of text reconstruction and generation jointly determine what the continuous representation should retain, while the discrete generator handles the residual uncertainty that the latents do not explain. Specifically, Cola2 dynamically segments text into semantic spans, controls the compression rate with an auxiliary-loss-free negative-feedback mechanism, and combines reconstruction and generation supervision to learn compact and predictive latent representations. On the discrete side, block-causal masked diffusion model (MDM) decoder [1, 41] is jointly trained under clean, noisy, and dropped latent conditions, balancing semantic reconstruction with context-based autonomous generation, and classifier-free guidance (CFG) [15] adjusts this balance at inference. During training, the token-prediction loss is backpropagated through the latents to the encoder, so that the continuous representation and discrete generation co-adapt; the Diffusion Transformer (DiT) [38] learns the current latent distribution via Flow Matching [26] without backpropagating gradients to the encoder, thereby decoupling prior fitting from representation learning. At inference, the model re-encodes the generated text block by block under the fixed span layout, keeping the latent history consistent with the actual text context and aligning the two spaces throughout generation. Building on these ideas, we systematically study co-adaptive hierarchical language generation across continuous and discrete spaces from three perspectives: probabilistic modeling, representation learning, and generation performance. Our main contributions are as follows: We propose Cola2, co-adaptive hierarchical language modeling framework. From the perspective of conditional information decomposition, we analyze semantic compression, the reconstructiongeneration balance, and continuousdiscrete co-adaptation in unified manner, clarifying the relation between the information retained by the latents and the residual left to discrete generation. We develop generation-oriented joint learning mechanism for continuous and discrete representations. It combines dynamic semantic compression, generation-oriented supervision, and training under latent 2 conditions of varying reliability, and coordinates representation learning with prior fitting through gradient decoupling, so that compact semantic representations and discrete generation capability co-evolve. We validate the core designs and their scaling potential through systematic experiments. Controlled five-task scaling to about 210B tokens and separate 346.03B-source-token pretraining run show competitive, unsaturated scaling. The latter reaches 60.10 average over eight tasks and surpasses Llama-3-8B on HellaSwag and StoryCloze despite over 43 fewer reported tokens, demonstrating decoder capability transfer and compatibility with autoregressive and masked-diffusion token-space generators.

sections.title: 2.1 Semantic Compression and Hierarchical Language Models
sections.content: Fixed-granularity methods shorten the modeled sequence through chunking or downsampling [33, 48]. Adaptive compression methods dynamically aggregate bytes or tokens according to content [18, 36, 39]. Concept-level methods organize generation through sentence representations or concept prediction [3, 7]. In contrast, Cola2 maintains the target compression rate through negative-feedback control without an auxiliary compression-rate loss, and combines reconstruction and generation supervision to learn compact and predictive continuous semantic representations.

sections.title: 2.2 Token-Space Language Models
sections.content: Autoregressive methods generate text serially, token by token [6, 11, 45]. Discrete diffusion methods predict multiple positions in parallel through iterative denoising [2, 27, 34, 41, 42, 47], and have been further extended to block-level generation and token editing [1, 4, 5]. Continuous-augmented methods use paired continuous states to assist discrete denoising [44, 51, 52]. In contrast, Cola2 learns semantic prior in compressed latent space and then performs conditional generation with discrete decoder, handling semantic modeling and text realization hierarchically.

sections.title: 2.3 Continuous Representations and Latent-Space Language Models
sections.content: Token-aligned methods perform diffusion or flow modeling on continuous representations [8, 10, 12, 16, 22, 23, 46]. Autoencoder-based latent-space methods separate latent generation from text decoding [28, 29, 50]. Joint-learning methods further co-optimize the latent space and the generative model [13, 30]. In contrast, Cola2 drives representation learning with discrete reconstruction and generation supervision while isolating the prior-fitting gradient, so that semantic compression and the decoders reconstructiongeneration balance are optimized jointly.

sections.title: 3 Cola2: Continuous Latent Diffusion for Hierarchical Text Modeling
sections.content: We formulate hierarchical text generation as continuous latent-variable model and, from an informationdecomposition perspective, discuss semantic compression, the reconstructiongeneration balance, and continuous discrete co-adaptation (Section 3.1). We then present the unified model, training procedure, latent-feedback inference procedure, and computational cost (Sections 3.23.3).

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: Following the training pipeline in Section 3.2, our experiments address three questions: (1) how to build compressed latent space that is semantically rich and easy to model; (2) how to train the latent generator; and (3) how the decoder should allocate its capacity between conditional reconstruction and autonomous generation.

It is trained on OLMo 2 pretraining data retokenized with the Qwen3-4B tokenizer, using length-4096 sequences. The decoder and the VAE encoder embedding are initialized from Qwen3-4B-Base. During decoder training, masked positions are represented by [MASK] inputs, while decoder self-attention remains causal. Stage trains the dynamic-compression VAE on 52.43B source tokens. Stage II jointly updates the VAE and an approximately 4B-parameter latent DiT, with detached VAE latents, on an additional 125.83B source tokens. Stage III freezes the Stage-II EMA VAE and continues training only the DiT on 167.77B source tokens. The total is 346.03B source tokens. Architecture, optimization, objective, EMA, and state-transition details are provided in Appendix I. sections.title: 5 Limitations & Future Prospects
sections.content: Although our results provide initial evidence for the feasibility, competitiveness, and scaling potential of Cola2, we view the current system as starting point rather than finished endpoint. First, the model remains far from convergence, especially the latent DiT, while the present training scale is limited by available resources. Larger models, longer training, and broader data and compute budgets are therefore needed to establish its performance ceiling. Second, compression reduces the dominant linear and attention FLOPs of the latent prior in theory, but end-to-end generation speed also depends on the decoder, CFG branches, latent feedback, and hardware utilization. Infrastructure co-designincluding specialized kernels, cache management, and parallel schedulingis needed to translate theoretical savings into practical speedups. Third, Cola2 already shows compatibility with autoregressive and masked-diffusion decoders, but their co-training objectives, inference trade-offs, and optimal division of labor remain underexplored. Finally, the continuous latent space may provide shared interface between text and other continuous modalities such as vision, opening path toward unified latent representations, cross-modal priors, and unified understanding and generation.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: We presented Cola2, hierarchical language modeling framework that unifies dynamic semantic compression with balanced discrete reconstruction and generation through continuousdiscrete co-adaptation. Dynamic compression and generation-oriented supervision encourage compact, predictive latent representations, while the decoder realizes latent semantics and handles residual uncertainty from context. Token-prediction gradients drive encoderdecoder co-adaptation, whereas latent-prior fitting remains decoupled from representation learning. Systematic component analyses and controlled evaluations on five downstream tasks, scaled to about 210B training tokens, support these design principles and show competitive, unsaturated scaling. In separate resource-constrained run, the final checkpoint trained on 346.03B source tokens achieves 60.10 average over eight tasks and surpasses Llama-3-8B on HellaSwag and StoryCloze, although that baseline reports over 43 more pretraining tokens. These results indicate successful transfer of the Qwen-initialized causal decoders generation capability and substantial scaling headroom, especially because the latent DiT remains far from convergence. More broadly, Cola2 shows that continuous-latent hierarchical modeling can integrate effectively with established token-space generators, including autoregressive and masked-diffusion decoders, rather than depending on single decoder paradigm.

(3.5) in the main text holds: H(Y C) = I(Y ; ZA C) + H(Y C, ZA). (E.1) The cond state uses the complete clean latent and therefore typically provides the most informative condition for the current block. The drop state zeros the latent condition of the current block, which corresponds to masked token prediction that does not depend on that latent. The noise state applies small random perturbation to the clean latent to train the decoders robustness to imprecise conditions. Together, the three states cover three training regimes: strongly conditioned reconstruction, local robustness, and weakly conditioned generation. For any discrete generator decoder pψ(Y C, ZA), the cross-entropy decomposes exactly as LA(ψ) = H(Y C, ZA) + KL(q(Y C, ZA)pψ(Y C, ZA)) . (E.2) The first term is determined by how much uncertainty remains under the given condition; the second is the modeling error of the finite-capacity discrete generator decoder relative to the optimal conditional distribution. Training only under cond mainly optimizes the strongly conditioned region and may make the model overly dependent on precise latents, whereas training only under drop may cause the discrete generator decoder to ignore the latent. Mixing cond, noise, and drop trains the same decoder parameters to reduce the modeling error across different levels of condition reliability. Final-Checkpoint Pretraining Recipe This section describes the large-scale recipe used for the final checkpoint in Table 4. It is separate from the matched component and controlled scaling setup in Section 4.1. I.1 Shared Training Configuration The pretraining corpus uses OLMo 2 pretraining data retokenized with the Qwen3-4B tokenizer. The sequence length is 4096. All stages use AdamW with β = (0.9, 0.95) and weight decay 0.01. The EMA decay in Stages II and III is 0.9998. At stage boundaries, model parameters, optimizer state, the learning-rate scheduler, and the data cursor are restored. I.2 Stage I: Dynamic-Compression VAE Stage processes approximately 52.43B source tokens. Dynamic segmentation compresses about two tokens into one latent on average, with maximum span length 8 and latent dimension 64. The decoder is initialized from Qwen3-4B-Base, and the VAE encoder embedding is copied from the same model; the remaining compression modules are initialized from scratch. The Qwen-initialized parameters remain frozen for the first 5.24B source tokens and are subsequently updated at 0.1 the main learning rate; the compression encoder also uses 0.1 multiplier. The learning rate is linearly warmed up from 106 to 104 over the first 5.24B source tokens and then cosine-decayed to 106. The decoder uses causal dual-stream objective. Masked positions are supplied as [MASK] inputs, but the decoder self-attention remains causal rather than becoming bidirectional. Clean, noisy, and dropped latent conditions are sampled with proportions 0.4/0.3/0.3, and their three token-loss weights are all 1. The KL, duration, and encoder-mask auxiliary loss weights are 104, 0.1, and 1, respectively, and the encoder-mask span ratio is 0.15. I.3 Stage II: Joint VAE and Latent-DiT Training Stage II restores the complete VAE checkpoint, optimizer, scheduler, and data cursor from Stage I. It introduces an approximately 4B-parameter latent DiT with 34 Transformer layers, hidden dimension 2560, 20 attention heads, and latent block size 8. This stage processes approximately 125.83B source tokens. The VAE continues to use the Stage-I causal dual-stream objective, with the encoder-mask span ratio increased to 0.30. The DiT reads detached VAE latents, so its diffusion loss does not backpropagate into the VAE; the VAE is updated only by its compression and decoder objectives. The DiT uses velocity-prediction MSE, with timesteps sampled from LogitNormal(loc = 2, scale = 1). The DiT learning rate is warmed up from 106 to 1.5 104 and then cosine-decayed. The schedule is defined over nominal 2.1T-token horizon, although training terminates before reaching that horizon. I.4 Stage III: Frozen VAE and Continued DiT Training Stage III restores the complete DiT parameters, EMA, optimizer, learning-rate scheduler, and data cursor from the Stage-II checkpoint. The Stage-II EMA VAE encoder is frozen, and only the DiT continues to be optimized. The released model uses the matching EMA VAE decoder associated with this encoder. The timestep distribution remains LogitNormal(loc = 2, scale = 1).
